opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think it was a very genuine phase. When I was younger, especially as a student, I had this strong urge to write things down and put them out there. Some of it was about research, some about random thoughts on life, technology, or whatever I happened to be reading. There wasn't much calculation behind it. It felt natural: you think about something, you get excited, and you want to share it with whoever might be listening.

Now when I reread some of those old posts, honestly, a lot of it is a bit embarrassing. You can see how naive I was and how confidently I said things I didn't fully understand. But I don't regret it. That kind of expression helped me figure out what I actually cared about. Writing forces you to organize your thinking, and sometimes you only discover what you believe after you've written it down.

Over time that urge changed. Once you're in academia or industry and people start paying attention to what you say, you become more careful, sometimes too careful. You think about how things will be interpreted and whether a casual comment will be taken out of context. In some ways that's maturity. In other ways I miss the freedom of just saying what I thought without worrying about it.

So I see that period with a mix of nostalgia and self-awareness. I think it's still important to keep some of that original impulse: the curiosity, and the willingness to put half-formed ideas out there and let people push back. A lot of good research starts from exactly that kind of open, slightly reckless sharing.

r001.rationale: The response describes spontaneous writing and sharing, but never says he deliberately cultivated melancholy to have something poetic to write.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I look back at it now, I feel a little embarrassed, but also kind of grateful.

I started writing online when I was still a student, and at that time there was no real audience. I wasn't writing because I thought I had something important to say. I was writing because I was confused, and putting things into words was the only way I could figure out what I actually believed. A lot of it was half-digested ideas about research, about papers I had just read, about why some direction felt right and another felt wrong. If you went back and read those posts, I think you'd find they're mostly wrong, or at least naive.

But that urge to express yourself, I think it's actually important, and not just as a personal habit. In research, there's a huge gap between understanding something in your head and being able to explain it clearly to someone who hasn't lived inside the problem with you. Blogging forced me to close that gap over and over. It taught me that if I couldn't write it simply, I probably didn't understand it yet.

The other thing is that it connected me to people. In the early days, the Chinese machine learning community online was quite small. You'd write something, and some stranger would leave a long comment disagreeing with you, and then you'd go back and forth for a week. Some of those people became collaborators, some became friends. That kind of open argument shaped how I think about science, that ideas should be out there, exposed, and that being corrected in public is not a humiliation but a gift.

I'll admit the motivation wasn't entirely pure. There's a part of any young person who writes online that wants to be seen, wants recognition. I had that too. What changed over time is that I became less interested in being right and more interested in being useful. Now when I write or post something, I ask myself: does this help someone think more clearly, or is it just noise? I think my younger self was producing a lot of noise. But without that noise, I don't think I would have learned to find the signal.

r001.rationale: The response describes writing from confusion and learning through blogging, but does not say he deliberately cultivated melancholy to have something poetic to write.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think a lot of it was wanting to put my thoughts somewhere and see whether anyone connected with them. When you’re younger, you don’t necessarily have a clear distinction between having an opinion and having something worth saying. Writing can help you discover that distinction—you start explaining something and realize you haven’t actually thought it through.

There’s also a desire to be understood. You’re figuring out what interests you, and putting it online creates the possibility that someone will say, “I’ve been thinking about that too.” So I wouldn’t dismiss that urge, even if I might express things differently now. The useful part is the willingness to make your thinking visible and let it change through conversation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses wanting to share thoughts and be understood, but does not say he deliberately cultivated melancholy to have something poetic to write.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think I was trying to figure out what I thought. When you’re young, you encounter something interesting, or something bothers you, and you want to put it into words. Posting it online gives that process an audience, even if the audience is very small.

There’s also a desire to be understood—to find people who resonate with what you’re thinking. But I wouldn’t want to describe every post as having some deep purpose. Sometimes you just have an opinion and want to say it. Looking back at those things can be embarrassing, but that’s part of growing up. You don’t have to agree with your younger self to appreciate that willingness to express something.

r001.rationale: The response discusses expressing opinions and wanting to be understood, but does not recall deliberately cultivating melancholy to have poetic material to write about.
